input:
## Scope
This review sets out to survey the published work on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation over the last 11 years, drawing together a total of 84 papers that report a catalyst tested for the conversion of carbon dioxide with hydrogen and that provide sufficient experimental detail for the underlying test conditions to be recovered. The reaction families that fall within the scope of the review are methanol synthesis, the reverse water-gas shift reaction, and methanation. Electrochemical and photochemical conversion, by contrast, fall outside the scope, as do reaction sequences in which hydrogenation represents just one step among several and the catalyst is not characterised in its own right.

The material classes covered by the review are copper-based catalysts, iron-based catalysts, noble-metal catalysts, and oxide catalysts. The overwhelming majority of the papers are laboratory-scale studies, carried out in fixed beds at pressures, temperatures, and feed compositions that were selected by the original authors rather than harmonised across the field. This lack of a common basis inevitably limits what any review can realistically do with the 84 papers: results can be placed side by side and claims can be compared, but catalysts cannot simply be re-ranked on a single scale, because no single scale runs consistently through the underlying reports. Where a paper reports a quantity on a basis that other papers do not share, the review records the basis alongside the quantity and leaves the comparison open, rather than forcing an alignment that the source material does not support.

## Established results
A number of findings recur across different groups and across different material classes, and it is these findings that this section treats as established. First and foremost, the preparation route appears to decide a great deal of what a catalyst actually does: for copper-based materials, the way in which the copper is distributed in the support at the start of the test emerges as the strongest single predictor of the activity that is reported at the end of it, and catalysts that begin with copper finely divided tend to hold their advantage over catalysts that begin with copper in larger grains. Promoters, meanwhile, seem to change selectivity considerably more than they change activity. Across both the copper and the iron classes, a promoted catalyst and its unpromoted counterpart will generally convert carbon dioxide at broadly comparable rates while sending the products in quite different proportions, and claims to the effect that a promoter raises activity itself generally do not survive a careful check of the conversion at which the comparison was actually made.

Stability is the second major established theme, and it is a somewhat less comfortable one. Every material class covered in the review loses performance on stream, whether through sintering, through oxidation-state drift, through fouling, or through some combination of these mechanisms that the original authors were unable to separate. Water that is formed by the reaction is implicated in a great deal of this loss: the various classes differ markedly in how much water they can tolerate, and this difference appears to be a property of the class as a whole rather than of any individual preparation. Supports, furthermore, are by no means inert in this respect. A support that succeeds in holding a catalyst's active phase in place under a dry feed may well fail to do so under a wet one, and several well-known results in the field are, on closer re-reading, results about supports just as much as they are results about active phases. The reverse water-gas shift reaction and methanol synthesis also divide the classes in a relatively settled way: iron-based materials are the default choice where the shift reaction is the objective, and copper-based materials where methanol is the objective, and this particular division is one of the few points on which the literature does not appear to argue with itself.

## Disagreements
The disagreements in the literature are concentrated, to a large extent, on one particular quantity: the methanol selectivity that is reported at a stated conversion. Different groups working with closely similar copper-based catalysts report selectivities that differ by margins which no straightforward reading of the test conditions can explain. Part of this conflict is essentially a matter of accounting. Selectivity is reported on different bases across the 84 papers, with some groups counting carbon monoxide as the product of a side reaction and others treating it as an intermediate and excluding it altogether, and the two conventions inevitably move the reported number without any change whatsoever in the underlying catalyst. Where the convention is explicitly stated, the conflict narrows considerably; where it is not, the numbers simply cannot be reconciled from the published record, and this review makes no attempt to reconcile them.

Beneath this first conflict there runs a second one: whether the oxidation state of copper under reaction conditions is the quantity that actually decides methanol selectivity, or whether it merely tracks it. The evidence that is offered on each side is drawn from characterisation that was carried out either before or after reaction rather than during it, and the two camps tend to read the same spectra in rather different ways. The review takes no position on this question beyond recording what would actually settle it, namely a measurement of the working catalyst, under feed, at the conditions of the test itself. Measurements of that kind are rare in the papers covered by this review, and their rarity is, in itself, something of a finding about the current state of the evidence base.

## Gaps
Arguably the most important gap is a measurement that nobody appears to report: catalyst performance over an extended period of time on stream under a feed that carries with it the impurities of an industrial carbon dioxide source. The papers covered in this review test with clean feeds, over durations that are convenient for a laboratory programme, and report activity and selectivity from the early, stable-looking portion of the run. An industrial plant, however, offers none of these conveniences. Its carbon dioxide arrives either from a capture unit or from a process stream, complete with traces of whatever the upstream process happens to carry, and its catalyst is expected to go on performing for far longer than any test reported in the 11 years covered here. Whether the rankings that have been established on clean feeds would survive a realistic feed is simply unknown, because the experiment has not been carried out in a form that the literature records.

The second gap is a reporting gap rather than an experimental one. Test conditions that are capable of deciding a result, including the exact feed composition, the pretreatment that was applied, and the convention lying behind a reported selectivity, are missing from a substantial share of the papers, and it is their absence that turns what might have been recoverable differences into permanent disagreements. The adoption of a common reporting basis, of the kind that other branches of catalysis have already adopted, would cost the field very little, and would transform the next review of this literature from an excavation into a comparison.

Several classes recover part of their lost performance when the fouling or the oxidation-state drift is reversed, and none recovers all of it; the unrecovered part is the part that accumulates over a campaign, and it is the unrecovered part that a plant lives with. Reports that quote recovery without separating the two parts overstate the durability of every class alike.

## Disagreements
The disagreements in the literature concentrate on one quantity: the methanol selectivity reported at a stated conversion. Groups working with closely similar copper-based catalysts report selectivities that differ by margins no reading of the test conditions explains. Part of the conflict is accounting. The same habit of reading across bases affects the activity comparisons, though less severely: conversions are quoted at contact times that differ between groups, and a catalyst compared at a shorter contact time is being compared at a different point of its own behaviour. The review flags those comparisons where the published record allows the contact times to be recovered, and passes over them where it does not.

## Gaps
The gap that matters most is a measurement nobody reports: catalyst performance over extended time on stream under a feed that carries the impurities of an industrial carbon dioxide source. The papers in this review test with clean feeds, for durations that suit a laboratory programme, and report activity and selectivity from the early, stable-looking part of the run. A common reporting basis, of the kind other branches of catalysis have adopted, would cost the field little and would make the next review of this literature a comparison rather than an excavation. Until one of the two gaps closes, the findings of this review are best read as findings about catalysts under laboratory conditions: sound on preparation, on promotion, and on the direction of the disagreements, and silent on the question a plant would ask first.
